lessons.title: Welcome to BookBot
lessons.readme:
# Welcome to BookBot

This is probably your first Python project, and almost certainly your first one on Boot.dev. Nice.

We're building **BookBot**, a Python program that analyzes novels and reports their word and character counts. You will:

- Set up a local Python development environment on your computer.
- Build a complete project from scratch.
- Work in a professional code editor ([Zed](https://zed.dev/) recommended).

> [!tip]
> While you're learning, we recommend **not** using inline AI tab completion in your code editor.

Here's what you'll build (you might want to go fullscreen):

![bookbot demo](/media/storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/lesson_videos/bookbot-final-project-demo-1920x1080-1920x1080.mp4)

## [!windows] Windows Users

> [!warning]
> Our automated tests run in Linux and macOS environments. On Windows, run the Boot.dev CLI inside [WSL 2](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/install), not a plain Windows terminal.

## Boot.dev CLI

You'll use the [Boot.dev CLI](https://github.com/bootdotdev/bootdev?tab=readme-ov-file#installation) to test work on your machine. You'll find each lesson's CLI commands in the test panel. The CLI has two modes:

- `bootdev run <id>` runs checks without submitting.
- `bootdev run -s <id>` submits your work and marks the lesson complete when it passes.

## Assignment

1. [ ] [Install the Boot.dev CLI](https://github.com/bootdotdev/bootdev?tab=readme-ov-file#installation) if you don't already have it. The installation instructions and troubleshooting steps are on that page.
2. [ ] Verify the installation:
   ```sh
   bootdev --version
   ```
3. [ ] Log in and follow the prompts:
   ```sh
   bootdev login
   ```

**Submit** the lesson from the test panel. There's no penalty on failure for this lesson.

lessons.title: Workspace
lessons.readme:
# Workspace

Many programmers spend _years_ writing code without developing a system for organizing it. They end up with project directories scattered across their filesystem.

> [!lane]
> I know it sounds silly, but it gets painful to manage so many projects. That's why I use the system I'm about to show you.

You can organize your code however you prefer, but this method has served me well. It's similar to how Go used to _enforce_ workspace organization, which mirrored how code projects are hosted online:

`~/workspace/USERNAME/PROJECTNAME`

For example:

- `~/workspace/bootdotdev/curriculum`
- `~/workspace/wagslane/go-rabbitmq`

This keeps _all_ my projects in a predictable location on my system.

_Adopt my system if you'd like, but you don't have to._

## Assignment

Regardless of how you organize your code, create a project [directory](<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directory_(computing)>) for BookBot. This directory will be the root of your project.

# Readme

A [`README.md`](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/managing-your-repositorys-settings-and-features/customizing-your-repository/about-readmes) is a [Markdown](https://www.markdownguide.org/getting-started/) file that explains what a project does and how to run it.

> [!lane]
> And if you're a _real developer™_ then it's always out of date and doesn't provide enough info.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Create a file named `README.md` in your editor and copy this text into it (be sure it matches, we'll be checking):

   ```md
   # bookbot

   BookBot is my first [Boot.dev](https://www.boot.dev) project!
   ```

   > [!info]
   > The `[anchor](link)` syntax is how you make a link in Markdown.

2. [ ] Save the file ([[Cmd]]+[[S]] on macOS, [[Ctrl]]+[[S]] on Windows/Linux).

**Run and submit** the CLI tests _from the root of your project_.

lessons.title: Installing Python
lessons.readme:
# Installing Python

Until now, you've written Python in the _browser_. Install Python 3 on your computer so you can run BookBot locally.

## Assignment

Follow the instructions for your operating system.

### [!linux][!windows] Windows (WSL 2) / Linux Users

You may already have Python 3 installed. Check by running:

```sh
python3 --version
```

If that worked, skip to the submission step.

If the command failed and you're using Ubuntu (including WSL 2's default distribution) or Debian, install Python 3 with [`apt`](https://documentation.ubuntu.com/server/how-to/software/package-management/):

1. [ ] Update the available package list and install Python 3:
   ```sh
   sudo apt update
   sudo apt install -y python3
   ```
2. [ ] Verify the installation:
   ```sh
   python3 --version
   ```

If your Linux distribution doesn't use `apt`, install Python 3 with its package manager, then run `python3 --version`.

**Submit** the CLI tests. There's no penalty on failure for this lesson.

### [!macos] macOS Users

We'll use the [Homebrew](https://brew.sh/) package manager to install Python 3.

1. [ ] Check whether Homebrew is installed:
   ```sh
   brew --version
   ```
2. [ ] If that command failed, install Homebrew:
   ```sh
   /bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"
   ```
3. [ ] Follow any post-installation shell instructions that Homebrew prints, then restart your shell.
4. [ ] Install Python 3:
   ```sh
   brew install python
   ```
5. [ ] Verify the installation:
   ```sh
   python3 --version
   ```

That command should print a Python 3.x version.

**Submit** the CLI tests. There's no penalty on failure for this lesson.

lessons.readme:
# Running Python

Let's run some Python code! We'll pass a script's file path to the [`python3` command](https://docs.python.org/3/using/cmdline.html#interface-options).

## Assignment

1. [ ] Create a file called `main.py` using your editor's file explorer, or this command:
   ```sh
   touch main.py
   ```
2. [ ] Add the following line of code to `main.py`, then save the file:
   ```py
   print("greetings boots")
   ```
3. [ ] Run your program:
   ```sh
   python3 main.py
   ```

If the script printed `greetings boots` to the console, your local Python environment is working!

**Run and submit** the CLI tests _from the root of your project_.

# Book Data

BookBot needs a book to analyze. We'll start with Mary Shelley's _Frankenstein_, which is in the public domain.

lessons.title: Read File
lessons.readme:
# Read File

Now let's start _ackshually_ building BookBot by reading the contents of _Frankenstein_.

## Open and Read a File

Use a [`with` block](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/compound_stmts.html#with) with the built-in [`open()` function](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#open):

```py
with open(path_to_file) as f:
    file_contents = f.read()
```

The [`f.read()` method](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/inputoutput.html#methods-of-file-objects) returns the file's contents as a string.

_The `with` block will automatically close the file when the block exits, cleaning up resources._

## Assignment

1. [ ] Delete your "greetings boots" message.
2. [ ] Write a function called `get_book_text()`. It should accept a file path as a string and return the file's contents as a string.
3. [ ] Write a `main` function that uses `get_book_text()` with the _relative_ path to your `frankenstein.txt` file to print the entire contents of the book to the console.
4. [ ] Call `main()` at the bottom of your file to execute your program.
5. [ ] Test your program:
   ```sh
   python3 main.py
   ```

**Run and submit** the CLI tests from the root of your project.

## Tips

- File paths are strings, so remember to put the path in quotes.
- A relative path starts from your current working directory. Because you're running the program from the project root, the path to the book starts with `books/`.
- You don't _need_ to write all your functions and variable names the same as mine; I'm just trying to give you some examples of how you can _potentially structure your code_. There are many correct ways to write the same program.

lessons.title: Count Words
lessons.readme:
# Count Words

Time for our first bit of data analysis! Let's count the words in the book.

## Splitting a String

The [`str.split()` method](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#str.split) splits a string on [whitespace characters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitespace_character) like spaces and line breaks by default. It's an easy (though not entirely accurate) way to break a string into a list of words.

```py
words = "Books are fun".split()
print(len(words))
# 3
```

The [`len()` function](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#len) then gives a word count.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Write a new function that accepts the book's text as a string and returns its word count as an integer.
2. [ ] Instead of printing the book's contents, print this message:

   ```text
   Found {num_words} total words
   ```

   Replace `{num_words}` with the book's actual word count.

**Run and submit** the CLI tests from the root of your project.

lessons.title: Refactor
lessons.readme:
# Refactor

[Refactoring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_refactoring) is a fancy word for improving your code's _structure_ without changing its _behavior_.

There are different kinds of refactoring. Here, we'll split the code in `main.py` across two smaller modules.

## Importing

In Python, each `.py` file is a **module**. You can bring functions, variables, and classes from one module into another with an [`import` statement](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/simple_stmts.html#import). A module's name is just its filename without the `.py` extension.

For example, a `database.py` module might contain a `connect` function and a `db_version` variable. You could import both into `main.py`:

```py
from database import connect, db_version
```

We'll organize BookBot with this structure:

- `main.py`: The program's entry point and file-reading logic
- `stats.py`: Functions that analyze the text

## Assignment

1. [ ] Create a new `stats.py` file, then move your word-counting function from `main.py` into `stats.py`.
2. [ ] Import the function into `main.py`. For example, if you named it `get_num_words`, the import should look like this:
   ```py
   from stats import get_num_words
   ```

**Run and submit** the CLI tests from the root of your project.

lessons.title: Count Characters
lessons.readme:
# Count Characters

Character counts are the core of BookBot's analysis. We'll store them in a dictionary where each key is a character and each value is the number of times it appears.

To get accurate totals, we can convert all characters to lowercase with the [`.lower()` method](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#str.lower). That way uppercase and lowercase letters share one count. Spaces and symbols should also be included in the dictionary.

For example, `"Boot!"` produces:

```py
{"b": 1, "o": 2, "t": 1, "!": 1}
```

## Assignment

1. [ ] Add a function to `stats.py` that accepts the book's text and returns a `dict[str, int]` containing the count of every character, including spaces and symbols. Convert each character to lowercase with `.lower()`.
2. [ ] Import and call the function in `main.py`, and capture the result in a new variable.
3. [ ] After printing the word count, print the dictionary of characters and their counts.

**Run and submit** the CLI tests from the root of your project.

lessons.title: Organize Data
lessons.readme:
# Organize Data

Right now, our character counts are stored in a dictionary. That's perfect for counting, but the final report needs the characters ordered from most common to least common.

To do that, we'll convert the dictionary into a list of `(character, count)` tuples, then sort the list by count.

## Sorting Lists

You can use the built-in [`sorted()` function](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#sorted) to sort a list. It returns a _new_ sorted list:

```py
counts = [7, 10, 2]
sorted_counts = sorted(counts)
print(sorted_counts)
# [2, 7, 10]
```

If you want the biggest values first, use `reverse=True`:

```py
counts = [7, 10, 2]
sorted_counts = sorted(counts, reverse=True)
print(sorted_counts)
# [10, 7, 2]
```

For BookBot, we're not sorting a simple list of integers. We're sorting a list of tuples, and we want to sort by the count _inside_ each tuple. We can control how `sorted()` compares items by passing a helper function to the `key` parameter:

```py
def sort_on(vehicle: tuple[str, int]) -> int:
    return vehicle[1]


vehicle_counts = [("car", 7), ("plane", 10), ("boat", 2)]
sorted_vehicle_counts = sorted(vehicle_counts, reverse=True, key=sort_on)
print(sorted_vehicle_counts)
# [('plane', 10), ('car', 7), ('boat', 2)]
```

The `key=sort_on` part tells `sorted()` to call `sort_on` for each tuple and use the returned value for comparison. In this example, that means we're sorting by the number at index `1` in each tuple.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Add a helper function called `sort_on` to `stats.py`.
   - It should accept a `tuple[str, int]` like `("b", 4868)`.
   - It should return the count value from the tuple – the second value.
2. [ ] Add a new function called `chars_dict_to_sorted_list` to `stats.py`.
   - It should accept the `dict[str, int]` returned by your character-counting function.
   - It should return a `list[tuple[str, int]]`.
3. [ ] Inside the new function, create an empty list.
4. [ ] Loop over the dictionary's keys.
   - For each character, look up its count in the dictionary.
   - Append a tuple to the list, like `("b", 4868)`.
5. [ ] Sort the list _from greatest to least_ by _count_.
   - Use the built-in [`sorted()` function](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#sorted).
   - Pass your `sort_on` helper as the `key`.
   - Use `reverse=True`.
6. [ ] Return the sorted list.
7. [ ] Import and call `chars_dict_to_sorted_list` in `main.py`, and capture the result.
8. [ ] Replace the character-count dictionary in your print output with the new sorted list.

For now, print the raw sorted list of tuples. We'll format it into the final report in the next lesson.

**Run and submit** the CLI tests from the root of your project.

## Tip

When sorting tuples, Python normally compares the first value first, then the second value if there's a tie. So we _could_ store our data as `(count, character)` and sort it without a `key`:

```py
chars = [
    (4868, "b"),
    (44538, "e"),
    (25894, "a"),
]

print(sorted(chars, reverse=True))
# [(44538, 'e'), (25894, 'a'), (4868, 'b')]
```

For BookBot, we'll keep each tuple as `(character, count)` because that shape is easier to read. The `key=sort_on` argument lets us sort by count without rearranging the data to fit Python's default tuple sorting behavior.

lessons.title: Print a Report
lessons.readme:
# Print a Report

Our data is organized; now it's time to print a pretty report!

The character-count dictionary includes spaces, punctuation, and other symbols that don't belong in the report. We can filter those out using the [`str.isalpha()` method](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#str.isalpha), which returns `True` when a string is non-empty and all of its characters are alphabetic:

```py
"a".isalpha()
# True

"!".isalpha()
# False
```

## Assignment

**Print the report in this format:**

```text

```

1. [ ] Add a `print_report` function to `main.py`.
   - It should take the book path, word count, and sorted list of character counts as inputs.
2. [ ] In `main`, replace your existing print calls with a call to `print_report`.
3. [ ] In `print_report`, print the report header, the book path, and the word count section.
4. [ ] Still in `print_report`, print the character count section.
   - Loop over the sorted list of characters.
   - Use [`str.isalpha()`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#str.isalpha) to _skip_ non-alphabetic characters.
   - Print each alphabetic character and its count in the format shown above.
5. [ ] Print the closing `END` line.

lessons.title: Arguments
lessons.readme:
# Arguments

BookBot is done! Almost...

You've probably noticed that most CLI tools you use (`ls`, `cd`, etc.) are not limited to a single "hardcoded" input. Right now, `bookbot` can _only_ analyze `books/frankenstein.txt`. That's not very useful.

Let's update the program so we can pass in any book path instead of using a hardcoded value.

## System Arguments

Python's built-in [`sys` module](https://docs.python.org/3/library/sys.html) provides access to [command-line arguments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Command-line_interface#Arguments) in the terminal. In particular, [`sys.argv`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/sys.html#sys.argv) is a list of strings representing the arguments passed to the script.

The first item in the list is the script name; the rest are the arguments. For example, `python3 main.py` creates a `sys.argv` list that looks like this:

```py
print(sys.argv)
# Prints ['main.py']
```

And `python3 main.py books/frankenstein.txt` creates a `sys.argv` list that looks like this:

```py
print(sys.argv)
# Prints ['main.py', 'books/frankenstein.txt']

print(len(sys.argv))
# Prints 2

print(sys.argv[0])
# Prints 'main.py'

print(sys.argv[1])
# Prints 'books/frankenstein.txt'
```

## Assignment

1. [ ] Remove any hardcoded book paths from your code. We'll get the path from the command instead.
2. [ ] At the top of `main.py`, import the built-in `sys` module:
   ```py
   import sys
   ```
3. [ ] In your code, check if the `sys.argv` list has at least two entries. If it doesn't:
   - [ ] First print a message explaining how to use the program: `Usage: python3 main.py <path_to_book>`
   - [ ] Then exit the program with a status code of `1` using [`sys.exit(1)`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/sys.html#sys.exit)
4. [ ] Use the second argument in `sys.argv` as the path to the book file instead of the hardcoded path.
5. [ ] Test your program with `python3 main.py books/frankenstein.txt` and make sure it works as expected.
6. [ ] Download some more books and test your program with them, adding them to the `books` directory and passing in their paths as CLI arguments when you run the program. Add at least these two books:
   - [ ] [`books/mobydick.txt`](https://storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/mobydick.txt)
   - [ ] [`books/prideandprejudice.txt`](https://storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/prideandprejudice.txt)

   > [!warning]
   > Use the books that are linked above, or the CLI tests will fail.

   You can also run the following commands from the project root to download and create the files:

   ```sh
   mkdir -p books
   curl -L "https://storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/mobydick.txt" -o books/mobydick.txt
   curl -L "https://storage.googleapis.com/qvault-webapp-dynamic-assets/course_assets/prideandprejudice.txt" -o books/prideandprejudice.txt
   ```

**Run and submit** the CLI tests from the root of your project.

If the tests pass, it means you've finished building BookBot. Congrats!

I hope you enjoyed this project. It's always good to solidify the things you learn in courses by getting your hands dirty with something practical.
